title: Prophecy Builds Up the Church
english: …to hear, or what profit will the words bring? For no one will understand except God alone, who knows all things. “For he speaks mysteries in the Spirit,” he says (1 Corinthians 14:2). Notice how the one who speaks to God speaks in the Spirit: so the Spirit is God. Therefore the one who speaks in a tongue, he says, speaks to God rather than to men; “but the one who prophesies speaks to men for building up, encouragement and consolation” (1 Corinthians 14:3).

Knowing, then, that “to prophesy” here means interpreting the writings of the prophets, through which the word of encouragement is made sure and the mind of those being instructed in the mysteries is led by the hand to the truth concerning Christ, he shows in another way as well that interpreting the prophets ranks incomparably higher than speaking in a tongue. “The one who speaks in a tongue,” he says, “builds up himself” (1 Corinthians 14:4), for he understands, but no one else at all does. But the one who uses the words and predictions of the holy prophets as testimony builds up the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). So prophesying is the greater thing and belongs among the highest grounds for boasting and among bright hopes, if indeed it is admittedly better to build up the church than to speak in a tongue to oneself alone.

“Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy,” and so on (1 Corinthians 14:5). It was something wonderful and truly God-given that men who were Hebrews could speak the languages of others. So that no one would think the apostle was rashly passing judgment on what had happened, by calling worthless what had been bestowed through the working of the Spirit (for it was given as a sign to believers), he welcomes the thing and says, “I want you all to speak in tongues.” But at once he plainly cuts short their eagerness for it and turns them to what is better, adding immediately, “but even more to prophesy,” and stating most clearly that the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue (1 Corinthians 14:5). Yet he shows that the gift is not altogether useless either to those who have it or to those who hear, when he adds, “unless he interprets” (1 Corinthians 14:5), that is, unless he has someone always at his side to interpret for those being instructed in the mysteries.
Tome Five. Discourse Three.

“And none of them is voiceless” (1 Corinthians 14:10). Some people used to come into the churches who had been enriched, by the working of the Spirit, with the ability to speak in tongues. Then, when they ought to have offered the prayers in the churches, and before these the litanies or the psalmody, using the language of those present, which they were able to do, they did not do it. Priding themselves only on the gift of tongues, they offered neither prayers nor psalmody. Paul teaches this: if the hearers do not know the language in which the one who has the gift is speaking, nothing is gained from it. For there are countless nations and many human languages, and none of those once counted among rational beings, or among men, is voiceless.

He says that none of those counted among rational beings, that is, among men, is altogether voiceless. But if someone does not know the meaning of another’s speech, and the others in turn do not know his language, they will be foreigners to one another (1 Corinthians 14:11), even though each speaks correctly in his own tongue. So those who wish to teach others must utter speech familiar to their hearers. But if the sound has no clear meaning and the speech is unfamiliar, he has labored in vain, merely striking the learner’s ear with an empty noise (1 Corinthians 14:9).

Those who wish to teach, he says, must speak in words familiar to their hearers, since otherwise one labors in vain; for speaking in tongues alone does not build up the church. “For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays” (1 Corinthians 14:14). By “spirit” here he means the grace given through the…

title: Praying with the Mind
english: …Spirit, that is, the ability to speak in tongues. So if, he says, I offer the prayers in the churches “in the spirit,” that is, using the tongue given through the Spirit, my mind will be unfruitful (1 Corinthians 14:14). For in prayer one must be intent and seek from God what leads to salvation, not pride oneself on a tongue and give oneself over merely to speaking in a tongue, since then the mind becomes unfruitful and gains no benefit from such display.

“I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). So, he says, if I choose to pray in a tongue, that is, to win esteem by speaking in a tongue, I must take earnest care not to have an unfruitful mind, and not to give myself over only to speaking in the tongue, but to rouse my mind within me. And if I happen to sing in a tongue, I must sing no less with the mind as well, by understanding the meaning of the psalmody and of the prophecy, and not leave such words unexamined (1 Corinthians 14:15). For if I utter empty sounds, “I have become a noisy gong” (1 Corinthians 13:1). So it is better to prophesy, that is, to interpret the divine Scriptures in church, than to be fond of merely using tongues.

What, then, will be the better way? “I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Here again by “spirit” he means the gift given through the Spirit. Since his aim, through a great many compelling arguments, is to show that speaking in a tongue is useless unless the ability to make the prophets plain to others goes with it, he adds still further points, in which one can see him saying it clearly.

“Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say the ‘Amen’?” (1 Corinthians 14:16). When you speak in a tongue, he says, how will the one who stands in the rank of the layman, if he does not know your language, answer “Amen” at your thanksgivings, that is, your prayers? For it is plain to everyone that in the churches the custom is for the prayers of those in the leaders’ charge to end together with the prayers of the leaders. They answer “Amen,” closing their own supplications to God at the priest’s words, so that whatever seems lacking in the people’s measure may be made up by the perfection of the priests, and so that God may receive, as it were, “the small together with the great” (Psalm 115:13) as in unity of spirit. For the people in their charge, joining their own prayers to the prayers of the priests, have believed that these will be accepted.

With this aim, too, God commanded that even poor sacrifices be brought to the altar of burnt offerings, so that the small, mixed with the perfect, might become acceptable to God. For we are all one in the Lord. So when you speak in a tongue, he says (for this is what “blessing with the spirit” means), how will the one who does not know what you are saying say the “Amen” at your thanksgiving? You yourself will do well, at least by the understanding that is in you, but the other is not built up (1 Corinthians 14:16–17). Yet everything we do must be done for building up and for the benefit of the brothers (1 Corinthians 14:26).
Tome Five. Discourse Four.

“Now I make known to you, brothers, the gospel that I preached to you” (1 Corinthians 15:1). Very aptly and wisely he calls the preaching about the resurrection of the dead, and surely also about the resurrection of Christ himself, a gospel, for it truly is the announcement of every good thing to those who have received the faith. And he says that they stand in it and are being saved (1 Corinthians 15:1–2). “To stand” signifies that believers are firm in hope and well established in glory, while “to be saved” signifies that they have even been shown…

title: Christ Died, Was Buried, and Rose
english: …superior to sin itself, and to have run beyond the snares of death. “For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3).

He says that he delivered to them, not something that had simply come into his mind and been accepted without testing, but the gospel that he received, since the one who became man for our sake put the knowledge of it into him. For the same apostle says again of the gospel, “For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:12). If, then, the one who hands it on is taught by God, how can what he preaches not be true: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3), that is, both the Old and the New?

For the witnesses of Christ’s death and resurrection are very many, so that it can no longer be doubted in any way that Christ Jesus died for us according to the flesh, to take away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and that he rose again, trampling on death, so that we too might gain this. Here he necessarily says not only that he died but also that he was buried (1 Corinthians 15:4). For Emmanuel was laid in a tomb to confirm that he had truly died; yet he came back to life, as I said just now. By dying in the flesh he gave full assurance that the Word, though he is God, had become flesh (John 1:14); and by trampling on death he showed plainly that he is God by nature.

Yet the Word who is from God the Father does not give life to a temple foreign to him, nor simply to that of someone else, but rather to his own body, through which he is also said to have died for us, so that the good of the resurrection too might be found to have truly come about for us. For the whole of human nature was in him, trampling on death; this is how we are said to have been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:12), and seated with him “in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6).

So he says that he was raised in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4), and that he appeared to the holy apostles, to some of them separately, as chosen ones, and also to a great number at once (1 Corinthians 15:5–7). “And he appeared also to me,” as to the one untimely born among the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:8). He speaks very humbly: he insists that he persecuted the church, but that he received mercy from Christ and was called to be an apostle (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). And he shows that the great mystery of the resurrection was not unknown either to the saints of old, for it had been foretold, or to those chosen for apostleship, who also “became eyewitnesses and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:2).

“Now if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Corinthians 15:12). He is astonished at those who, I do not know how, have been persuaded to set themselves against the holy and divine Scriptures and dare to think something other than this. For if Christ died, not to remain dead, but so that, proving stronger than death and corruption, he might become a kind of way and door for human nature (John 14:6; John 10:9), so that it could prevail over corruption and run back to life, then how, now that he who for our sake was among the dead has been raised, so that we too might rise with him to life, can they still bind in the snares of death those for whose sake Emmanuel, who is God by nature, is said to have died and come back to life?

Why do they rob the human race of the good things that come from the resurrection, and slander the goal of his saving work in the flesh? For if Christ has become “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20) and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18), then surely what remains will follow its own firstfruits and will go along with the firstborn, and with good reason, in keeping with what a firstborn is understood to be. And the inspired Paul himself will bear witness, saying, “For if…” (Romans 6:5).
